config.title: Write a custom map polyfill

intro.title: Write a custom map polyfill
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a custom version of JavaScript's built-in `map` method from scratch, called a polyfill. You'll learn how `map` works under the hood by creating a function that iterates over an array, applies a callback to each element, and returns a new array with the transformed results. The core concepts involved are array iteration, callback functions, and handling edge cases like empty arrays. This exercise will help you understand functional programming patterns and how to extend JavaScript's native capabilities.
intro.usecase: The map method is a foundational tool for data transformation in real-world applications. For instance, in an e-commerce dashboard, developers use map to convert raw product data into formatted display objects for a product grid. Similarly, in a form builder, map processes an array of field configurations to render interactive input components. Understanding how to implement a custom map polyfill deepens your grasp of functional programming patterns essential for building scalable, data-driven UIs.

objectives: Construct a custom function that replicates the core behavior of the native Array.map method.
Implement the custom map function to accept a callback as an argument.
Initialize a new array within the function to store transformed elements.
Manipulate array indices and elements by applying the callback to each item.
Control the execution flow to iterate through the original array without using built-in iteration methods.
Integrate the custom map function into a sample script to transform data.
Configure the callback to receive current element, index, and original array parameters.

steps.title: Understand the native map method
steps.instruction: Create a function named demonstrateNativeMap that logs the native map method's behavior to the console.
steps.hint: Define a function that creates an array, uses the native map method on it, and logs the result.

steps.expectedOutcome: A function is created that demonstrates how the native Array.prototype.map() method transforms an array.
successCriteria: The function demonstrateNativeMap exists and uses the native map method on an array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it uses the native map method on an array and logs the result.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function demonstrateNativeMap isn't properly defined or doesn't demonstrate the native map method. Try creating a function that uses array.map() and logs the result.

steps.title: Create the polyfill function structure
steps.instruction: Create a function called myMap that takes a callback function as its first parameter.
steps.hint: Define a function named myMap with a parameter for the callback.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a function named myMap that accepts a callback parameter.
successCriteria: The myMap function is defined and takes a callback parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined a function named myMap with a callback parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match what we need. Create a function called myMap that takes a callback parameter.

steps.title: Add the 'this' context parameter
steps.instruction: Add a second parameter named 'thisArg' to your myMap function to handle the optional 'this' context.
steps.hint: The native map method accepts an optional second argument that sets the 'this' value for the callback. Add this parameter after the callback parameter in your function definition.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your myMap function should now have two parameters: callback and thisArg.
successCriteria: The myMap function signature includes both 'callback' and 'thisArg' parameters.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added 'thisArg' as the second parameter in your function definition.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check your function signature. The myMap function should have two parameters: callback and thisArg.

steps.title: Initialize the result array
steps.instruction: Inside the myMap function, create an empty array at the beginning to store the mapped results.
steps.hint: Declare a variable with a descriptive name (like 'result' or 'mappedArray') and set it to an empty array [].
steps.expectedOutcome: The myMap function will have an empty array variable ready to collect transformed values.
successCriteria: An empty array variable is declared at the start of the myMap function body.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've declared an empty array variable at the beginning of the myMap function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The step requires creating an empty array variable inside the myMap function to store results. Try declaring a variable like 'const result = [];' at the start of the function.

steps.title: Get the length of the array
steps.instruction: Inside the myMap function, store the length of the array (this.length) in a variable named length.
steps.hint: You can get the length of the array using this.length and assign it to a variable.
steps.expectedOutcome: The myMap function will have a variable that holds the length of the array for use in the upcoming loop.
successCriteria: A variable named length is declared and assigned the value of this.length inside the myMap function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're storing this.length in a variable named length inside the myMap function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The step requires storing the array length in a variable. Look at the hint and try again.

steps.title: Create the loop structure
steps.instruction: Inside the myMap function, add a for loop that iterates from index 0 up to (but not including) the array length.
steps.hint: You'll need to use the length variable you stored in the previous step. The loop should have a counter variable (like i) that starts at 0 and increments while it's less than the length.
steps.expectedOutcome: The myMap function now contains a for loop structure ready to iterate through each element.
successCriteria: A for loop is added inside myMap that iterates from index 0 to length-1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your loop syntax. Make sure you're using the length variable and the loop runs from 0 to length-1.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loop structure isn't quite right. Remember to create a for loop that starts at index 0 and continues while the index is less than the array length.

steps.title: Check for existing elements
steps.instruction: Inside the for loop in your myMap function, add an if statement that checks whether the current index exists in the array using the 'in' operator.
steps.hint: The 'in' operator checks if a property exists in an object. For arrays, you can use 'index in this' to check if the index exists before calling the callback.
steps.expectedOutcome: The myMap function will correctly handle sparse arrays by only calling the callback for indices that actually exist in the array.
successCriteria: The for loop contains an if statement that uses the 'in' operator to check if the current index exists in the array before processing.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the 'in' operator to check if the index exists in the array. The syntax should be something like 'if (i in this)'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The step requires adding an if statement inside the loop that checks if the current index exists in the array using the 'in' operator. Try adding: 'if (i in this) { ... }' inside your for loop.

steps.title: Call the callback function
steps.instruction: Inside the for loop, after the if statement, call the callback function with three arguments: the current element (this[i]), the current index (i), and the original array (this). Store the result in a variable.
steps.hint: Remember that the callback function expects the element, index, and array as parameters, just like the native map method.
steps.expectedOutcome: The callback function will be called for each existing element in the array, receiving the element, its index, and the original array as arguments.
successCriteria: The callback is called inside the loop with three arguments: this[i], i, and this. The result is stored in a variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling the callback with all three arguments: the current element, the index, and the original array.
steps.feedbackWrong: The callback function needs to be called with three arguments: the current element (this[i]), the current index (i), and the original array (this).

steps.title: Return the result array
steps.instruction: Inside the myMap function, return the result array at the end of the function.
steps.hint: After the for loop completes, you need to return the array that contains all the transformed values.
steps.expectedOutcome: The myMap function should now return the array containing all transformed values from the callback.
successCriteria: The myMap function includes a return statement that returns the result array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning the array that contains the transformed values.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't return the result array yet. Add a return statement at the end of the function.
